title: When they don't want the book to end
author: Mary Myatt
summary: Mary Myatt reports on a conversation with two leaders at Meridian High School in Croydon about the new Year 7 foundation curriculum they launched in September. About 40 per cent of each incoming cohort arrive below the expected standard at Key Stage 2, so leaders built a phased transition, designed for the whole year group rather than an intervention group. Pupils receive 60 hours of focused work in reading, writing, oracy, spelling and numeracy before Christmas, with a graduation ceremony in December. Reading is central, using the Faster Read approach and carefully chosen award-listed books, and pupils have been asking for sequels and spending far more at the book fair. Early signs include better attendance and fewer behaviour incidents, though Myatt stresses these are only a few weeks of observations and a second round of assessment in December will show academic progress.
points: The school treated weak primary outcomes as a reason to build on local primary teaching rather than lower expectations, keeping ambition high while making the material reachable.
The foundation curriculum covers the entire Year 7 cohort, with books and tasks tailored to starting points identified through assessments in reading, maths, spelling and handwriting.
Reading is at the heart of the model, with book choices made for emotional resonance and intellectual stretch.
Pupil appetite is the early evidence, including requests for sequels and a book fair that took about 650 pounds compared with the usual 100.
Myatt is careful to call the results early observations, with proof of academic progress awaiting the December assessments.
quotes: When pupils ask for the next book in a series, something important is happening.

Around 40% of pupils in each incoming cohort arrive without having met expected standards at Key Stage 2. Historically, this gap created a persistent barrier as pupils moved through the curriculum towards their GCSEs.
Designed for the entire Year 7 cohort rather than an intervention group, the provision tailors books and tasks to different starting points.
It represents a significant structural decision, resting on the conviction that establishing strong literacy and learning habits first makes the subject curriculum far more accessible later.
Pupils have begun debating predictions, challenging each other’s interpretations, and asking for sequels, a request one leader had not heard in nine years at the school.
The team has resisted lowering expectations, choosing instead to make ambitious material reachable.
A second round of assessments in December will provide clearer evidence of academic progress, but for now, pupils actively asking for the next book gives us something genuine to celebrate.
